name: Lansing
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Lansing, MI | Genstone
metaDescription: Lansing renovation contractor for investors: Eastside foursquares, Moores Park brick and post-war ranches scoped pre-offer and built to rental certification.
intro: Lansing’s rental and resale demand rests on employers that do not pack up and leave: state government, the hospitals, Michigan State University just across the line in East Lansing, and the GM assembly plants on the west and south sides. That steady base is why investors keep buying the city’s older frame houses, many of which were built for auto workers when REO and Oldsmobile ran the local economy. The catch is that those houses are now a century old, and the repair list behind a cheap purchase price can be long. Genstone Construction runs a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you see the rehab cost and how it compares with the finished value before you sign. After you close, the work follows an itemized scope with a draw schedule, a field manager is assigned to the house, and licensed local trades take out permits with the city. Nothing is paid upfront, and each draw follows finished work.
housingStock:
Lansing grew around the Grand and Red Cedar rivers, the Capitol and its factories, and the housing reflects each of those anchors. Old Town, on the north bank of the Grand, contains some of the city’s oldest homes, including nineteenth-century Italianate and Victorian houses mixed with later infill. The Eastside, stretching out along Michigan Avenue toward East Lansing, is a dense grid of frame foursquares, gable-front houses and bungalows from roughly the 1900s through the 1920s, with front porches, shallow setbacks and detached garages on alleys. The Westside and Genesee neighborhoods hold larger early-century homes built for professionals who worked downtown, along with Arts and Crafts houses with deep eaves and built-ins.

South of downtown, REO Town grew up beside the REO Motor Car Company plant, and its small worker cottages sit close together on narrow lots. Moores Park, near the river and the park of the same name, has handsome 1920s brick Tudors and colonials. Colonial Village and Potter-Walsh fill in with 1920s through 1940s colonials, Cape Cods and modest bungalows, while Groesbeck on the northeast side and much of the south side were built after the war with ranch houses, split-levels and slab or crawlspace foundations. Those later houses often hide their original oak floors under wall-to-wall carpet, which is a pleasant surprise for a rehab budget.

For a rehab, the older neighborhoods bring familiar Michigan problems: knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply piping, cast-iron stacks, clay laterals, lead paint and asbestos on old heating pipes. Basements in the pre-war houses are usually concrete block or brick on clay soil, and many show seepage at the cove joint and cracks where frost has worked on them. The post-war ranches are simpler, but original aluminum windows, undersized electrical services and tired ductwork are common.

commonIssues.title: Wet block basements on clay
commonIssues.body: Much of Lansing sits on dense clay that holds water against foundation walls. In the Eastside and REO Town, block basements frequently show efflorescence, stair-step cracks and water at the joint between floor and wall after a heavy rain or spring thaw. Many houses lack a working sump. Before finishing any basement space, we look at the grading, the downspout discharge and the drain tile situation, then price interior drainage and a sump if the walls are taking on water.

commonIssues.title: Century-old wiring and services
commonIssues.body: A large share of the Eastside and Old Town housing was wired with knob-and-tube or early cloth cable, then partially updated by owners over the decades. You can find a modern breaker panel feeding old circuits behind the plaster. Lansing Board of Water & Light supplies power in the city, so a service upgrade means coordinating the meter and service drop with BWL. We price rewiring based on what we find when outlets and fixtures are opened, not on what the panel looks like.

commonIssues.title: Converted and chopped-up layouts
commonIssues.body: Near downtown, the Capitol and Michigan Avenue, some larger houses were divided into apartments or rooming units during the decades when government workers and students needed cheap housing. Those conversions often added kitchens without proper venting, cut new doors through bearing walls and ran wiring through closets. If you plan to keep the units, or to put the house back to one family, expect the hidden alterations rather than the finishes to set the budget, and open a few walls before you commit to a number.

commonIssues.title: Floodplain houses near the rivers
commonIssues.body: Parts of Lansing near the Grand and Red Cedar rivers, including portions of the Urbandale neighborhood on the east side, sit in mapped floodplain and have flooded in the past. Houses there may have water damage hidden in basements and wall cavities, and substantial renovation can trigger floodplain rules on elevation and repair. Check the flood zone, flood insurance cost and any past flood claims before you buy, because they affect both rent and resale.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint on porches and windows
commonIssues.body: Nearly all of the Eastside, Westside and REO Town housing predates 1978, and the front porches, window sashes and exterior trim that give those streets their character are where lead paint fails first. Peeling porch ceilings and chalking window wells are common findings. Rental inspections look for deteriorated paint, and any rehab that sands, scrapes or demolishes painted surfaces needs lead-safe work practices and careful cleanup before a family moves in.

investorMarket:
Lansing’s investors tend to sort themselves by neighborhood. The Eastside is the city’s most active area for small investors. Its walkable streets, proximity to Michigan Avenue and East Lansing, and stock of affordable older houses make it a good fit for both long-term rentals and modest flips aimed at young buyers who work downtown or at the hospitals. REO Town has similar small houses and has gained attention as its commercial strip filled in with restaurants and businesses.

Moores Park, the Westside, Genesee and Colonial Village draw owner-occupant buyers who want character homes at prices below East Lansing and Okemos. Those neighborhoods support fuller renovations, especially for brick Tudors and colonials with original details. Groesbeck and the south side offer post-war ranches that are easier to rehab and appeal to buyers who prefer one-floor living.

BRRRR and rental strategies work across the city because the tenant pool is broad: state employees, health care workers, plant workers, graduate students and young families. Investors focused on undergraduates usually buy in East Lansing instead, which has its own rental licensing rules and stricter occupancy limits. Ingham County Land Bank properties offer another path into the market, often with rehab requirements attached to the sale.
permits:
In the City of Lansing, building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are handled by the Building Safety Office within the Department of Economic Development and Planning. Most rehabs beyond cosmetic finishes require at least one trade permit. Rewiring, panel upgrades, new plumbing fixtures or water heaters, furnace replacements, structural changes, new windows that change opening size and roof work involving sheathing all fall in that category. Each permit includes rough and final inspections.

Rental property in Lansing must be registered, and units need a certificate of compliance that is issued after a code inspection. The inspection covers life safety devices, egress, heating, electrical hazards, plumbing and general property condition. Certificates are renewed on a recurring basis, so the property must stay up to code between tenants.

Neighboring communities each run their own departments. East Lansing has a separate rental licensing program, and townships such as Delta, Meridian and Lansing Township issue their own permits. Since a Lansing mailing address does not always mean City of Lansing jurisdiction, our field manager confirms who issues permits for the parcel before work is priced, then files every inspection result in your project folder.
climate: Mid-Michigan winters are cold and gray, with steady snow, frequent freeze-thaw cycles and stretches of deep cold that freeze pipes in unheated houses. Lansing sits far enough inland that it misses the heaviest lake-effect bands that hit the west side of the state, but snow and ice still accumulate on roofs, and ice dams form on older homes with poor attic insulation. Spring is often the riskiest season for rehabs. Snowmelt and rain saturate the clay soils, groundwater rises, and the Grand and Red Cedar rivers can flood low-lying areas. Summers are warm and humid, which feeds basement mold in houses with poor drainage. Exterior work such as roofing, siding, masonry and excavation is best scheduled from late spring through early fall.

faqs.q: Is the Eastside a good area for rental investors in Lansing?
faqs.a: Many investors focus there because purchase prices have been reachable and the location near Michigan Avenue, downtown and East Lansing attracts a wide range of tenants. The houses are mostly a century old, so the scope often includes wiring, plumbing, basement water and lead-safe paint work. Those items are predictable once you know to look for them, which is what our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed to catch before you commit.

faqs.q: Does Lansing require an inspection before I can rent a renovated house?
faqs.a: Yes. Rental properties in the city must be registered, and units need a certificate of compliance issued after a code inspection. Inspectors check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, egress, stairs and rails, heat, electrical safety and plumbing. We scope rental rehabs so those items are complete when construction ends, which helps you move from final permit inspection to rental certificate without a second round of repairs.

faqs.q: Do you work in East Lansing, Okemos and Delta Township?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates licensed contractors throughout the Lansing area. Each of those communities has its own building department, and East Lansing in particular has rental licensing and occupancy rules that differ from the city of Lansing. We confirm the jurisdiction before the scope is finalized so permit costs, inspection steps and any rental licensing requirements are reflected in the estimate and schedule.

faqs.q: How do lead water lines affect renovations in Lansing?
faqs.a: Lansing Board of Water & Light replaced its lead service lines years ago, so most houses in the city are not served by lead pipe at the street. Inside the house, though, older homes may still have galvanized supply piping that is corroded and restricts water pressure. We usually recommend replacing interior galvanized lines during a full rehab, especially if new bathrooms or kitchen fixtures are being installed.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Lansing, MI | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Lansing fix and flip contractor: Moores Park, Westside and Eastside homes estimated before you bid, renovated for owner-occupant buyers, paid as work is done.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Lansing
fix-flip.intro: Lansing flips sell to a particular buyer. Many are state employees, nurses, teachers and young professionals priced out of East Lansing and Okemos who still want an older house with some character close to downtown. They tend to buy with FHA or conventional loans, and their inspectors will open the electrical panel and look hard at the basement. Genstone Construction helps you build a flip that holds up to that scrutiny. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work on the house you are considering and compares it with the comparable sales you expect to sell against. Once you buy, a field manager runs the job from an itemized scope, licensed local contractors pull permits through the Building Safety Office, and draws are tied to completed stages so your money moves with the project.

sections.h2: Matching the finish level to Lansing neighborhoods
sections.body:
The same renovation does not fit every part of the city. In Moores Park, the Westside, Genesee and Colonial Village, buyers are looking at brick Tudors, colonials and Arts and Crafts homes, and they expect original woodwork, refinished hardwood, a well-designed kitchen and a bathroom that respects the age of the house. Spending on restoring built-ins and leaded windows can pay off there, because the competition in that price range often includes houses in East Lansing.

On the Eastside and in REO Town, the buyers are more often first-time purchasers who want a clean, updated house they can afford. A practical kitchen with durable counters, an updated bath, new flooring where hardwood cannot be saved, fresh paint and good lighting usually make more sense than high-end finishes. In Groesbeck and on the south side, ranch houses appeal to buyers who want one-floor living, and open kitchens and updated baths tend to matter more than period details. We compare your planned finish with the comps before we finalize the scope.

sections.h2: Passing the buyer’s inspection in a hundred-year-old house
sections.body:
Most Lansing flips fail at the inspection, not the showing. Buyer inspectors in this market regularly find knob-and-tube wiring still energized behind updated outlets, galvanized pipes with low flow, cast-iron drains with cracks, clay sewer laterals full of roots, and block basement walls with horizontal cracks or active seepage. A buyer who receives a long inspection report often asks for major credits or walks away.

We treat those items as part of the core scope. Replacing old wiring and adding grounded circuits, repiping supply lines, scoping the sewer and repairing it if necessary, correcting basement water with grading, downspouts and interior drainage, and documenting foundation repairs all help a flip close. Keeping receipts, permits and photos of that work gives the buyer’s agent something concrete to show their client. In Lansing, those records often carry more weight than another upgrade to the kitchen backsplash, and they reduce the risk of a renegotiation late in the deal.

sections.h2: Keeping a Lansing flip on schedule
sections.body:
Carrying costs add up month by month, and the biggest schedule risks in Lansing are hidden water damage, failed inspections and winter weather. A house that sat vacant through a cold season may have frozen supply lines or a cracked boiler. Basements that looked dry in August can take on water during the spring thaw.

Our pre-offer review and first site visit look for those problems early. The itemized scope lists every task with its cost and a draw schedule that follows the sequence of work: demolition, rough-ins, inspections, insulation and drywall, finishes and final inspections. The field manager sequences the electrician and plumber ahead of their inspections and holds the drywall crew until the rough-ins are signed off. When weather limits exterior work, we keep interior trades moving and schedule roofing, siding and concrete for warmer weeks. If hidden damage appears, you receive a change order with photos and pricing before anything is added. That keeps the schedule and budget predictable from purchase to listing.

faqs.q: Which Lansing neighborhoods support higher-end flips?
faqs.a: Moores Park, the Westside, Genesee and Colonial Village tend to support fuller renovations because they attract buyers looking for character homes at prices below East Lansing and Okemos. Even there, the finish level should match recent sales on nearby streets. We line up the scope against the sales on surrounding blocks, rather than adding upgrades the market may not pay for.

faqs.q: Should I finish the basement in a Lansing flip?
faqs.a: Only if it is dry and likely to stay that way. Many Lansing basements on clay soil take on water during spring thaw or heavy rain. Finishing over a damp wall invites mold and complaints after the sale. We look for signs of water, check the grading and downspouts and recommend drainage improvements first. In some houses, a clean, painted, dry basement is a better choice than finished space.

faqs.q: Do I need permits for a cosmetic flip in Lansing?
faqs.a: Purely cosmetic work like painting, flooring and replacing cabinets in the same location usually does not need a permit. Once you add circuits, move plumbing, replace a furnace or water heater, change windows or alter walls, permits are required. Buyers and their lenders may ask whether work was permitted, so we pull the permits needed for the actual scope through the city’s Building Safety Office.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Lansing, MI | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR contractor in Lansing: rehabs sized to the refinance appraisal and city rental certificate, with durable finishes for state, hospital and plant tenants.
brrrr.intro: Lansing has the ingredients investors look for in a BRRRR market: older houses that can still be bought below their renovated value and a tenant base anchored by government, health care, the university and auto plants. The plan only works if the rehab lifts the house enough to support the refinance while producing a rental that passes city certification and holds up to years of tenants. Genstone Construction plans the rehab around those three tests. Ahead of your offer, the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review puts a number on the rehab and weighs it against the value your lender will need to see. During construction, a field manager coordinates licensed local contractors from an itemized scope, permits run through the city’s Building Safety Office, and you release money only as each stage is complete.

sections.h2: Where Lansing’s BRRRR numbers tend to work
sections.body:
The best BRRRR candidates in Lansing are structurally sound houses that look worse than they are. On the Eastside, in REO Town and in parts of Baker-Donora and Potter-Walsh, you will find century-old frame homes with dated kitchens, worn floors, old furnaces and peeling paint. Buyers who want a move-in-ready house often skip them, which keeps purchase prices low enough for a refinance to make sense once the work is done.

Those same neighborhoods have steady rental demand. Tenants include state workers who want to be near downtown, staff at Sparrow and other medical centers, employees at the GM plants and graduate students who prefer Lansing rents to East Lansing’s. The challenge is that older houses carry more risk of hidden wiring, plumbing and foundation issues. Groesbeck and the south side offer post-war ranches with fewer surprises, though purchase discounts may be smaller there. We help you compare the expected repair cost, rent and post-rehab value across those options before you commit.

sections.h2: Rehabbing to the appraisal and the certificate
sections.body:
Two inspections follow your rehab: the appraiser for your refinance and the city inspector for your rental certificate. They look at different things, but the scope can satisfy both.

For the appraisal, condition and updates matter most. A new or newer roof, updated electrical panel and wiring, a high-efficiency furnace, a modern water heater, refinished or new flooring, a refreshed kitchen and bath, and a basement that stays dry all push the condition rating upward. We provide a detailed list of the improvements with photos so the appraiser can see what changed.

For the rental certificate, the inspector focuses on safety: smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, egress windows in bedrooms, railings on stairs and porches, safe electrical systems, working heat, sound plumbing and intact paint. In Lansing’s older housing, porch railings, basement stairs and window egress are common trouble spots. Building those items into the rehab from the start avoids a second visit from the contractor and keeps your refinance timeline intact.

A BRRRR rental has to perform for years after the refinance, and Lansing winters test every material. We recommend waterproof plank flooring in kitchens, baths and basements, where snowmelt and spills are common. If hardwood is in decent shape in living areas and bedrooms, refinishing it is usually better than covering it with carpet. Semi-gloss paint on doors and trim cleans easily, and solid-surface or quartz counters resist chipping.

Mechanical choices matter even more. A high-efficiency furnace and good attic insulation reduce tenant heating costs, which lowers turnover and late payments in winter. Replacing old galvanized supply lines prevents low pressure and leaks. Clearing gutters, extending downspouts and correcting grading help keep basements dry on clay soil. In houses with older block foundations, a sump pump with a battery backup can save you from an expensive cleanup after a spring storm. Each recommendation is tied to the rent you expect and to keeping the house in good shape for the next refinance or sale.

faqs.q: Will a Lansing rehab appraise high enough for a cash-out refinance?
faqs.a: It comes down to what you pay, what you put into the house and what similar homes on nearby streets have sold for recently. Before you write an offer, we price the rehab and set it beside the sales an appraiser would probably pull for an Eastside or REO Town house. When the margin between all-in cost and likely value is thin, you hear that from us up front, while you can still lower the offer or move on.

faqs.q: Should I buy BRRRR properties in Lansing or East Lansing?
faqs.a: Both can work, but they behave like different markets. East Lansing has higher purchase prices, strong undergraduate demand and a rental licensing program with occupancy limits that shape how many tenants a house can hold. Lansing offers lower entry prices and a broader tenant base drawn from government, health care and the plants. We can scope houses on either side of the city line so you can compare rehab cost, licensing steps and likely appraised value.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial help with the refinance?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit that can fit a BRRRR plan. You are free to use any lender with Genstone Construction. If you do use Genstone Financial, our detailed scope and draw records give the lender a clear view of what was done to the Lansing house, which can be useful when the refinance appraisal is ordered.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Lansing, MI | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Lansing rental renovation for single-family owners: certificate-ready rehabs, consistent portfolio specs, winter prep and turns coordinated by one team.
rental-renovation.intro: Single-family rentals are a big part of Lansing’s housing, especially on the Eastside, in REO Town and on the south side. Many are owned by investors who hold several houses and rely on a property manager to keep them occupied. Genstone Construction renovates and turns those homes using a consistent standard that fits Lansing’s housing stock and the city’s rental certification process. Every house still gets its own written scope and price, overseen by a field manager and built by licensed trades who are used to Lansing’s inspectors. Genstone Field Services can add inspections, occupied maintenance, make-ready work and code compliance so your rentals stay ready between renovations. Photos and status notes come to you, so a portfolio spread from Groesbeck to Baker-Donora can be managed from wherever you live.

sections.h2: Setting a rental standard for Lansing houses
sections.body:
Lansing portfolios often combine very different properties: a 1910s foursquare on the Eastside, a 1920s worker cottage in REO Town and a 1950s ranch on the south side. A good rental standard sets common materials and finishes while allowing for those differences.

Our usual Lansing spec puts waterproof plank in any room with a drain or an exterior door, carpet or refinished oak in the bedrooms, one wall color across the portfolio with washable trim paint, a fixed appliance model list and plain fixtures your maintenance tech can swap from the truck. Mechanically, it usually means high-efficiency furnaces, newer water heaters, updated electrical panels and GFCI protection in wet areas. In older homes, it also includes lead-safe treatment of windows and porches. A shared standard lets local contractors work faster because they know what to install, and it helps your property manager keep spare parts on hand. Over time, it also makes costs more predictable, because you can compare similar work across houses instead of starting from scratch each time.

The City of Lansing requires rental registration and a certificate of compliance issued after a code inspection. Certificates must be renewed, so each property will be inspected again. Many failures come from items that change between tenants: a smoke alarm removed, a handrail loosened, a window that no longer opens or paint that has started to peel.

We build certification items into renovations and turns. Before the next lease starts, the crew walks the house with the city’s checklist in hand, from the alarms and bedroom windows to the basement stair rail and the furnace. In older houses, basement stairs and porch railings are frequent trouble spots, and we repair them as part of the turn. Keeping a record of what was installed and when helps your property manager prepare for the next inspection. If the city cites an item, we can return quickly to correct it and help schedule the reinspection. That approach keeps your rentals legally occupied and reduces the risk of losing rent while repairs are made.

sections.h2: Turnover and winter in Lansing rentals
sections.body:
Turnover is where many rental portfolios lose money. A typical Lansing turn includes cleaning, paint touch-ups, flooring repair, appliance checks and fixing damage left behind. Since the spec is already written, a Lansing turn can be priced from a short walk-through and started within days of the keys coming back.

Winter adds risk. If a rental will sit vacant in cold weather, keep the heat on at a safe level or winterize the plumbing. A furnace failure in an empty house can freeze pipes within days. October is the month to get furnaces serviced, gutters emptied, downspouts carried away from the foundation and sump pumps tested. Because so many of these houses sit on clay, grading and downspout discharge get checked at every turn, not just when a tenant reports a wet basement. Ice dams can form on houses with poor attic insulation, damaging ceilings and walls, so we look at insulation and ventilation during turns. These steps cost far less than repairing water damage after a storm and help keep tenants comfortable through the coldest months.

faqs.q: Can several of my Lansing rentals be renovated at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes. Because we draw on a deep bench of licensed local trades, an Eastside foursquare, a REO Town cottage and a south side ranch can all be in progress during the same month. Each house keeps its own scope, budget and field manager attention, while your shared specification keeps the finishes and pricing aligned. Your property manager follows every address from one set of updates instead of fielding calls from separate crews.

faqs.q: Will you do repair work while my Lansing tenants are living in the house?
faqs.a: Yes. Occupied maintenance is part of what Genstone Field Services does. We set entry times through your property manager, tell tenants in advance when water or heat will be off, and keep outages short in cold weather. Because most rentals in the older neighborhoods have lead paint somewhere, crews contain dust and clean carefully whenever painted surfaces are cut or sanded, which protects the household and keeps the house in line with the city’s rental standards.

faqs.q: If a tenant breaks something, is that a warranty repair?
faqs.a: It is not. The one-year workmanship warranty is for problems with the work itself, like a shower valve that drips because it was installed poorly. A door kicked off its hinges, a carpet ruined by a pet or the slow wear of several years of living are a separate repair. We can photograph the condition at move-out, price the fix and give your property manager what they need to settle the deposit.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Lansing, MI
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Lansing duplex and 2–4 unit renovation: converted homes near the Capitol and Michigan Avenue, split utilities, fire separation and work around tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Lansing
multifamily-renovation.intro: Lansing’s small multifamily buildings are mostly houses that were divided. Near the Capitol, along Michigan Avenue and on the older streets of the Eastside and Westside, large homes were split into two, three or four apartments during decades when state workers, students and young families needed inexpensive rentals near downtown. The city also has purpose-built duplexes and a few small walk-ups. Investors who want several rents on one parcel bring us in to rework these buildings, and the planning starts with what the units share: the roof, the basement, the stairs, the utilities and sometimes a tenant who is staying. A field manager oversees the project, licensed local contractors pull permits through the Building Safety Office, and the scope is written so each unit can move toward its rental certificate as soon as it is ready.

sections.h2: What hides inside a Lansing conversion
sections.body:
Converted houses near downtown often look straightforward from the street, but inside they show decades of piecemeal changes. Kitchens were added in bedrooms and pantries, sometimes without proper venting. Bathrooms were squeezed into closets. New doors were cut through walls, and some of those walls carried load. Stairs to upper units may be steep, narrow or exterior and in poor condition.

Electrical systems are frequently overloaded, with one service feeding several units and circuits running through shared spaces. Plumbing stacks may serve multiple units, so a leak or clog in one apartment affects others. Fire separation between units is often weak or missing, with open chases and unsealed penetrations. Heating may come from a single old boiler or from multiple furnaces installed over the years. When we walk one of these buildings before you buy, the kitchens and floors get a glance and the attic, basement, panels and stairs get the hour, because the shared problems touch every unit and outweigh the cosmetic budget.

sections.h2: Safety and utilities in older multi-unit buildings
sections.body:
Safety and code compliance are the biggest drivers of cost in older Lansing multi-units. Upper units need safe, code-compliant egress, which may mean rebuilding exterior stairs or adding egress windows. Fire separation between units often requires fire-rated drywall, sealing penetrations and installing self-closing doors. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms must be added or updated.

Utilities are the other major decision. Buildings with a single boiler or one electric meter leave the owner paying for heat and power, which can be expensive in a Lansing winter. Separating utilities lets tenants pay their own bills. That may involve installing separate furnaces and water heaters, routing new ductwork, upgrading the electrical service and coordinating with Lansing Board of Water & Light for additional meters, plus extending gas piping to each new appliance. Each of those steps carries its own permit and inspection. Our plan covers the entire building, so you can see where equipment will go and what it will cost before you commit.

sections.h2: Working one unit at a time near downtown
sections.body:
Plenty of these buildings change hands with a long-time tenant downstairs and a vacant, worn-out unit above. That arrangement is workable if the order of work is planned. We start with whatever the occupied unit depends on: a roof that leaks into both floors, a sewer lateral that backs up into the shared basement, an overloaded service. Those jobs are booked as short, announced shutdowns, often on a single day, so the tenant knows when the water or power will come back.

The vacant unit then becomes a normal renovation with its own sequence of rough-ins, inspections and finishes. Crews come and go by the rear stair where possible, keep the front hall clear and protect shared floors. Lead-safe containment matters more here than in a single-family house because dust follows tenants up and down common stairs. Once the vacant unit passes its inspections and is leased, the occupied unit can be renovated at turnover with the first unit’s rent already coming in, and each apartment earns its certificate in turn.

faqs.q: Can a converted Lansing house be returned to single-family use?
faqs.a: In neighborhoods like the Westside and Genesee, a restored single-family house can sometimes outsell the same building as a rental, particularly when it still has its original staircase and woodwork. Reversing a conversion means confirming zoning, pulling permits, removing the added kitchens and reworking entrances and stairs. We price the building both ways, as units and as one home, so you can weigh resale against the rent roll.

faqs.q: How does Lansing’s rental certificate apply to a building with several units?
faqs.a: Every apartment has to meet the city’s rental requirements, and the halls, stairs and basement everyone shares are inspected too. On older conversions the problem spots are usually the rear stair, missing alarms between units, overloaded wiring and peeling paint in common areas. We sequence the work so a finished unit can be inspected and leased without waiting for the rest of the building, which shortens the time the property earns nothing.

faqs.q: Are multi-unit buildings in East Lansing handled differently?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is worth knowing before you buy. East Lansing runs its own building department and rental licensing, and its occupancy rules in many neighborhoods limit how many unrelated tenants can share a unit. That affects both the layout you renovate toward and the rent you can expect. We confirm which city the parcel is in and build the scope and permit plan around the rules that actually govern it.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Lansing, MI | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Lansing for buyers, agents and lenders: Limited and Standard bids, consultant coordination and documented draws.
fha-203k.intro: Lansing has many houses that are good buys but not quite livable: an Eastside foursquare with a failing furnace, a Colonial Village Cape Cod with a 1960s kitchen, a Moores Park Tudor with a leaking roof. The FHA 203(k) loan lets a buyer finance both the purchase and the renovation, which opens those houses to people who cannot pay cash for repairs. Genstone holds FHA 203(k) contractor certification, and in Lansing we work alongside buyers, their agents, loan officers and HUD consultants to produce the bid, the detailed scope and the draw paperwork the program depends on. A field manager oversees the renovation, licensed local trades work under city permits, and draws follow the loan’s schedule so buyers can see where every dollar of renovation money went.

sections.body:
The 203(k) works best on homes that are structurally sound but outdated. In Lansing, that includes Eastside foursquares and bungalows with old wiring and furnaces, REO Town cottages with tired kitchens and baths, Colonial Village and Potter-Walsh Cape Cods that have not been updated in decades, and post-war ranches in Groesbeck or on the south side with original windows and ductwork.

Moores Park and Westside homes can also be good candidates. Their brick Tudors and colonials often need roofing, masonry repairs and updated systems, and buyers value the character those homes offer. Converted multi-unit houses may qualify as well if the buyer will live in one unit, but they often require fire safety and egress work that makes the project more complex. Houses in the floodplain near the rivers need extra care, because flood zone requirements and insurance can affect the loan. During our review, we tell you whether the repair cost and expected value make sense together.

sections.h2: Why the basement usually decides Limited or Standard
sections.body:
On paper the choice is simple. The Limited 203(k) is for non-structural work and tops out at $75,000. The Standard 203(k) starts at a $5,000 minimum, covers structural repairs and brings in a HUD-approved consultant who writes up the work and inspects each draw, with added requirements once repairs pass the $15,000 inspection threshold.

In Lansing, the deciding factor is often below grade. A great many Eastside and REO Town houses sit on concrete block walls in wet clay, and a buyer who sees only a damp corner may be looking at a horizontal crack and an inward bow that needs anchors or a partial rebuild. That is structural work, and it moves the file to the Standard program. A house with a sound, dry basement and an outdated kitchen, furnace and roof usually fits the Limited version comfortably. Because switching loan types late costs the buyer time and fees, we examine the foundation on the first visit and mark every structural item in the scope so the lender can choose correctly at the start.

sections.h2: From bid to final draw on a Lansing file
sections.body:
The lender will size the loan from our bid, so it is written item by item: the furnace with its model class and venting, the electrical panel and the circuits it feeds, each window opening, each plumbing fixture, and the permit fee that goes with the work. On a Standard file, we compare it against the consultant’s write-up and resolve differences before closing.

Once the loan funds, the renovation money is held back and released stage by stage. For each draw, the field manager sends photos of the completed work, the passed Building Safety Office inspection for that stage and lien waivers from the trades who were paid. Lansing’s winter shapes the order: we try to close up the roof and exterior before the cold sets in, and save interior trades for the darker months. When hidden damage appears, like a rotted sill under old aluminum siding or a cast-iron stack that cracks when the bath is opened, the change order goes to the lender with photos before any extra work is done.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) be used on an Ingham County Land Bank house?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Land Bank homes vary widely, from houses that need paint and a furnace to shells that need everything, and the sale often comes with its own rehab conditions and deadlines. The deciding questions are whether the lender will finance the property and whether the finished value supports the total cost. Share the address with us and your loan officer, and we can produce a scope that answers both before you commit.

faqs.q: When should a Lansing buyer’s agent call a 203(k) contractor?
faqs.a: As soon as a client is serious about a house that needs work, ideally before the offer is written. A quick walk-through lets us flag the items that change the loan type, like foundation movement or a bearing wall the buyer wants removed, and give the agent a preliminary figure to work with. Starting early also means the lender has a bid in hand on time, which keeps the closing date from slipping.

faqs.q: Can work continue on a Lansing 203(k) through the winter?
faqs.a: Inside, yes. Electrical, plumbing, insulation, drywall, cabinets and flooring move along fine once heat is on in the house. Roofing, siding, exterior paint and concrete are more weather-dependent, so we try to get them done before the hard freeze or schedule them for the first workable stretch in spring. If the house is empty when the loan closes in cold weather, protecting the plumbing is the first task on the list.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Lansing, MI | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Lansing REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze-damaged Eastside homes, Urbandale flood history and rental-ready repairs, all photo-documented.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Lansing
reo-renovation.intro: A bank-owned house in Lansing could be a clean 1950s ranch in Groesbeck that needs carpet and paint, or a century-old Eastside foursquare that spent a winter with the gas shut off. The scope, the cost and the eventual buyer differ completely between the two, and the asset manager needs to know which one they have before approving a dollar. Genstone Construction renovates REO homes in the Lansing area for servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and the Government-Sponsored Enterprises, with whom Genstone holds preferred-contractor standing. Each bid is itemized and photographed, each property has its own field manager and licensed local trades perform the work under city permits. Genstone Field Services keeps the house secured, winterized and inspected while bids are reviewed, so the condition you approved is still the condition when work starts.

sections.body:
The first walk-through on a Lansing REO is about finding water, because almost every expensive problem here starts with it. In older Eastside and REO Town houses, frozen supply lines split in the first deep cold after the gas is shut off, and if the curb stop was left open the leak runs until someone notices. Plaster ceilings sag, hardwood cups and the basement fills. Clay soil and a dead sump pump add a second flood at spring thaw.

Roofs come next. Ice dams on poorly insulated houses push water into the top-floor walls, and a vacant house has nobody to notice the stain. Then the security items: forced doors, broken basement windows, missing copper and signs of squatting. Houses in the Urbandale area or elsewhere near the Red Cedar and Grand may also carry flood history from before the foreclosure. Each condition is photographed and tied to a bid line so the asset manager can see the cause behind the cost.

sections.h2: Repairing toward the buyer who will close
sections.body:
Who buys a renovated Lansing REO determines how far the repairs should go. Owner-occupants using FHA or conventional loans need a house with working heat, a roof that does not leak, safe wiring, rails on stairs and no peeling paint on a pre-1978 home. Investors, who are a large share of buyers on the Eastside and the south side, will need to register the property and pass a city rental inspection, so they discount houses with obvious code failures.

We scope to the buyer the listing broker expects, and we show the asset manager what a financeable baseline costs next to a fuller renovation. Neglected houses may also have open code enforcement cases for tall grass, trash or open structures, which we try to identify and close as part of the work. Any job in a mapped floodplain that rises to a substantial renovation can trigger additional floodplain review, so we raise that before the scope is final. Permits go through the Building Safety Office and closed inspections are saved to the file for the closing.

sections.h2: How we report to asset managers
sections.body:
Every Lansing bid is laid out the way an asset manager reviews it: one line per repair, labor and materials split, debris removal and dumpsters already counted, and a photo attached to each line. Trash-outs on long-vacant Eastside houses are often heavy, so leaving disposal out of the bid would understate the job.

While work is underway, the field manager reports progress against the approved lines rather than in general terms, which makes it easy to see what remains. If opening a wall reveals something new, such as charred framing from an old electrical fire or a cracked cast-iron stack behind the bathroom, the change order arrives with photos and a short explanation before work continues. Lien waivers are gathered from each trade at payment. Because preservation and construction sit in the same company, grass cutting, re-keying, utility transfers and periodic inspections are scheduled around the renovation instead of by a separate vendor who may not know the house is under construction.

faqs.q: What should be done first on a Lansing REO taken over in winter?
faqs.a: Stop the water. Confirm the curb stop is closed, drain and winterize the lines, check the water heater and boiler for freeze damage and make sure the sump has power ahead of the thaw. Genstone Field Services can secure the doors and windows and complete an initial condition report the same visit. If renovation will continue through the cold months, restoring heat early lets interior trades work and protects new plumbing.

faqs.q: Which REO clients do you work with in the Lansing area?
faqs.a: Our REO work in mid-Michigan is done for loan servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and the GSEs, which have named Genstone a preferred contractor. We adapt to each client’s bid template, photo rules and approval thresholds. On Lansing files, our notes also cover open code items, permit status and whether the house sits in a mapped floodplain, so the asset manager has a full picture before listing.

faqs.q: How do you handle REO homes in Lansing’s floodplain areas?
faqs.a: We check the flood zone before the scope is written and look for evidence of past water, such as tide lines on basement walls, swollen trim, replaced drywall at a consistent height and mold behind finishes. Damaged materials are removed and the structure is dried before rebuilding. If the work is large enough to count as a substantial improvement under floodplain rules, we tell the asset manager early, because that can change what the repair must include.
